title: OCD 15 — Test
src: Non-odontogenic tumors of the oral cavity

mcqs.q: Willis defined neoplasia as a proliferation that:
opts: Does not regress after the stimulus is removed
mcqs.explain: Neoplasia = abnormal, uncoordinated, purposeless proliferation that does not regress after removal of the evoking stimulus.

mcqs.q: Non-odontogenic tumours, by definition, do NOT arise from:
mcqs.explain: Non-odontogenic tumours arise from epithelium, connective tissue, muscle, nerve or vessels — not tooth-forming (odontogenic) tissue.

mcqs.q: The cause of a squamous papilloma is:
mcqs.explain: Squamous papilloma is a benign HPV-induced epithelial tumour.

mcqs.q: Squamous papilloma is classically associated with HPV types:
mcqs.explain: Benign papillomas are linked to HPV 6 & 11; HPV 16 & 18 are associated with neoplastic change.

mcqs.q: The typical clinical appearance of a squamous papilloma is:
mcqs.explain: It is a small (<1 cm) white, exophytic, cauliflower/granular growth, often on tongue or buccal mucosa.

mcqs.q: The histopathological hallmark of HPV infection in a papilloma is the:
mcqs.explain: Koilocytes (pyknotic nuclei within an optically clear halo) are the HPV cytopathic hallmark.

mcqs.q: HPV types associated with neoplastic (malignant) change are:
mcqs.explain: HPV 16 & 18 are high-risk types associated with neoplastic transformation (common in HIV).

mcqs.q: Focal epithelial hyperplasia is also known as:
mcqs.explain: Focal epithelial hyperplasia = Heck's disease (multifocal papillomavirus epithelial hyperplasia).

mcqs.q: Focal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck's disease) is caused by HPV types:
mcqs.explain: Heck's disease is caused by HPV 13 & 32; it is common in younger patients and in HIV.

mcqs.q: The microscopic hallmark of focal epithelial hyperplasia is the:
mcqs.explain: Mitosoid bodies (keratinocytes resembling mitotic figures from collapsed nuclei) are characteristic of Heck's disease.

mcqs.q: The usual clinical course of focal epithelial hyperplasia is:
mcqs.explain: Lesions are painless multiple papules that tend to regress spontaneously through immune response.

mcqs.q: A keratoacanthoma is characterised by:
opts: A symmetric crater filled with keratin
mcqs.explain: Keratoacanthoma is a well-circumscribed, symmetric crater filled with keratin, with squamous proliferation at the edges.

mcqs.q: Keratoacanthoma may:
mcqs.explain: Keratoacanthoma may regress spontaneously, though surgical excision is commonly performed.

mcqs.q: Oral squamous cell carcinoma accounts for approximately what fraction of oral cancers?
mcqs.explain: About 95% of oral cancers are OSCC; the other ~5% include melanoma, lymphoma and metastases.

mcqs.q: Which tumour-suppressor gene is classically lost in OSCC?
mcqs.explain: Loss of the p53 tumour-suppressor gene (with oncogene activation) drives OSCC.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the classic 'S' risk factors for OSCC?
mcqs.explain: The 'S' factors are smoking, smokeless tobacco, spirit, sepsis, syphilis, spices, sunlight and sharp tooth — not sucrose.

mcqs.q: Squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue most often arises on the:
mcqs.explain: The lateral (and ventro-lateral) border of the tongue is the commonest tongue site for OSCC.

mcqs.q: In the TNM system, T1 denotes a tumour:
mcqs.explain: T1 ≤2 cm; T2 2–4 cm; T3 >4 cm; T4 >4 cm with deep invasion of muscle/bone.

mcqs.q: A tumour larger than 4 cm without deep invasion is classified as:
mcqs.explain: T3 = tumour larger than 4 cm; T4 adds deep invasion of muscle/bone/deep structures.

mcqs.q: N1 nodal status describes:
opts: A single ipsilateral node smaller than 3 cm
mcqs.explain: N1 = single homolateral node <3 cm; N2 = 3–6 cm or bilateral; N3 = >6 cm.

mcqs.q: Broder's grading of OSCC is based on:
mcqs.explain: Broder's system grades histologic differentiation: well, moderately or poorly differentiated.

mcqs.q: The histological hallmark of a WELL-differentiated OSCC is:
mcqs.explain: Keratin (epithelial) pearls indicate keratinisation in well-differentiated OSCC.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised histopathological variant of OSCC?
mcqs.explain: Variants include verrucous, spindle-cell (sarcomatoid) and basaloid squamous cell carcinoma.

mcqs.q: Standard treatment of OSCC is guided by TNM/grade and combines:
mcqs.explain: Management combines surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy according to stage and grade.

mcqs.q: Peripheral giant cell granuloma is a reactive lesion arising from the:
mcqs.explain: PGCG is a reactive lesion from the periodontal ligament or periosteum, often after local trauma.

mcqs.q: The typical clinical appearance of a peripheral giant cell granuloma is a:
opts: Red-blue nodule on the gingiva/alveolar ridge
mcqs.explain: PGCG presents as a red-blue nodular lesion on the gingiva or alveolar ridge, commoner in women (5th–6th decade).

mcqs.q: Histology of a peripheral giant cell granuloma shows:
opts: Multinucleated giant cells and haemosiderin in a vascular stroma
mcqs.explain: PGCG shows multinucleated giant cells with haemosiderin deposits in a vascular stroma.

mcqs.q: A solitary circumscribed neuroma results from proliferation of:
mcqs.explain: Solitary circumscribed neuroma is a benign proliferation of Schwann cells within the nerve.

mcqs.q: Identify the white, cauliflower-like lesion shown.
mcqs.explain: A white, exophytic, cauliflower-like growth is a squamous papilloma (HPV 6/11).

mcqs.q: Identify this dome-shaped lesion with a central keratin-filled crater.
mcqs.explain: A symmetric crater filled with keratin and peripheral squamous proliferation is a keratoacanthoma.

mcqs.q: Identify the ulcerated lesion on the lateral border of the tongue.
mcqs.explain: A non-healing ulcerated/indurated lesion on the lateral tongue is highly suspicious for OSCC.

mcqs.q: This histology shows invasive squamous islands with keratin pearls — the diagnosis is:
mcqs.explain: Invasive islands of squamous epithelium with keratin pearls = well-differentiated OSCC.

saqs.a: An abnormal, uncoordinated, purposeless proliferation of tissue whose growth does not regress after the evoking stimulus is removed.

saqs.q: List four of the 'S' etiologic factors of oral squamous cell carcinoma.
saqs.a: Smoking, smokeless tobacco, spirit (alcohol), sepsis, syphilis, spices, sunlight, sharp tooth.

saqs.q: Contrast squamous papilloma and Heck's disease by HPV type and one histological feature.
A <1 cm white cauliflower lesion of the tongue shows koilocytes on biopsy. Diagnosis and causative virus?
Give the TNM for a 3 cm oral carcinoma with one ipsilateral 2 cm node and no metastasis.
saqs.a: T2 N1 M0 (T2 = 2–4 cm; N1 = single ipsilateral node <3 cm; M0 = no metastasis).
